More than 1,300 people are missing in Nepal and Tibet, including 47 Americans, after a glacial collapse caused catastrophic floods, with video showing mud sweeping through entire communities. Drone footage in Nepal showed roads destroyed and buildings buried by thundering water the color of wet cement. Nepalese authorities ramped up operations in the worst-affected districts of Nuwakot and Rasuwa. The disaster in Nepal and Tibet is not a one-off. The Lhende Khola river system has now flooded twice in just 14 months and the increasingly unstable Himalayan ice system threatens communities, infrastructure and water supplies across one of the world’s most densely populated regions. The region saw similar flash floods in August last year, when a glacial lake in Tibet overflowed because of high temperatures. Nine people were killed, and critical infrastructure, including a bridge connecting Nepal and China, was damaged.

🇳🇵 LOCAL SURVIVORS OF THE NEPAL FLOODS: THEY SURVIVED, BUT LOST ALMOST EVERYTHING For many local people, surviving the devastating floods was only the beginning of another struggle. 73-year-old Bhakta Lal Shrestha was at an elderly home in Devighat when the flood struck. He and more than 100 other residents were trapped for nearly nine hours before rescuers finally reached them. In Tupche village, 49-year-old Parbati Adhikari survived because she had left her village to visit a nearby temple before the flood arrived. When she tried to return, five bridges had already been washed away. She eventually found shelter with other survivors and was reunited with her husband and son. And 8-year-old Zoyal Ghale survived by running into the forest and climbing trees as floodwaters tore through his community. Injured and alone, he was eventually rescued and later reunited with his mother. These are more than numbers. They are mothers, fathers, children, grandparents and entire families who watched their homes disappear in minutes. Some survived. Some are still missing. The 2026 Nepal Flood Explained: Where Did All The Water Come From? (Part 1) On August 26, 2026, a catastrophic flash flood struck the Nepal-Tibet border, erasing infrastructure in a terrifying 13-minute window. Initial global reports blamed a simple earthquake or a glacial lake outburst—but satellite imagery and seismic data proved both theories completely wrong. In Part 1 of this forensic scientific investigation, we solve the central mystery: Where did millions of cubic meters of water suddenly originate in a valley with no lake? We analyze the 34-million-year-old metamorphic bedrock failure on Langtang Lirung at 5,200 meters, the physics of kinetic friction melting, the impact that pulverized a hidden lower-valley glacier, and how the resulting wave reached 160 km/h. Part 2 covering the secondary 4.2 earthquake, the ticking landslide dam, and the full downstream impact will be released next. The flooding was not simply ordinary monsoon flooding. A sudden ice/rock avalanche and collapse in the Himalayan region near Tibet caused a huge surge of water, mud, rocks and debris into the Bhote Koshi River. The resulting flash flood swept through villages and infrastructure with very little warning.  The worst-affected areas include Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading and Chitwan, with impacts also reported in Gorkha and Tanahun.  🕯️ Deaths and missing people The situation has continued to worsen as rescue teams recover bodies and update missing-person lists.
